title: UX Has a Basics Problem
intro: Choosing a checkbox over a radio button is a logic question, not a matter of taste. Teams that re-debate settled conventions waste hours and ship contradictions developers spot immediately.

learn.title: Three controls, three different logics
learn.text:
**Checkbox** — independent options. Zero, one or many. A single checkbox is one yes/no.

**Radio button** — exactly one of two or more mutually exclusive options.

**Toggle / switch** — a binary state that takes effect immediately, like a setting.

Each control signals a different logic. Picking the wrong one is a mismatch between what the interface says and what the system does.

try.q: A user must pick exactly one billing cycle: monthly or yearly. Which control?
options: Radio buttons
Two checkboxes
A toggle switch
A checkbox with a help icon explaining the rule
try.explain: Radio buttons mean exactly one of several mutually exclusive options.

left.label: Seen in review
items: Required email as a disabled switch

right.label: What the logic calls for
items: Plain text: you'll always get this

learn.title: The email preferences review
learn.text:
A single on/off switch was meant to control separate email and SMS checkboxes underneath it. Nobody could say what the switch should show when only one was ticked, or what toggling it would do.

A legally required email appeared as a preference with a **disabled switch** — offering a choice the user doesn't have.

The team spent close to an hour on questions that already had answers.

try.q: A legally required notification is shown as a greyed-out toggle. What is wrong with that?
options: It presents a choice the user doesn't have
Greyed-out controls fail colour contrast rules
Toggles should never be used for notifications
Legal notifications belong on a separate settings page entirely
try.explain: If there is no choice, say so in plain text instead of showing a disabled control.

learn.title: Raise the floor, not just the ceiling
learn.text:
The AI-era argument that designers bring “taste” usually means aesthetics. Calabro's order of work:

**user goals → real system states → real user choices → the pattern that fits → then the visual polish**

Re-debating settled conventions teaches the rest of the company that UX is common sense anyone can do.

try.q: Where does visual polish come in Calabro's order of work?
options: Last, after the pattern is chosen
First, to get buy-in from stakeholders
Alongside choosing the control
It isn't part of a designer's job at all
try.explain: Goals, states and choices decide the pattern; polish comes after.

test.q: Why does Calabro call control choice a logic question?
options: The control has to match what the system actually does
Logic puzzles are a good interview exercise for designers
Because engineers prefer logical arguments to visual ones
Because usability testing can't resolve questions of taste
test.explain: A mismatch between control and system state is an error, not a preference.

test.q: What does a single checkbox represent?
options: One yes/no choice
One of several exclusive options
A setting that applies immediately
A required field that cannot be skipped
test.explain: Checkboxes are independent: zero, one or many; a single one is a yes/no.

test.q: What is the cost of re-debating settled conventions, beyond the lost hours?
options: It teaches the company that UX is just common sense
It delays the visual design phase of the project
It makes the design system harder to maintain
It leaves junior designers without clear mentorship
test.explain: It devalues the discipline and ships contradictions developers spot immediately.

test.q: Which control is right for a setting that takes effect the moment it changes?
options: A toggle switch
A radio button
A checkbox
A dropdown with Apply and Cancel buttons
test.explain: A toggle is a binary state that takes effect immediately.

test.q: What does “raise the floor” mean in this article?
options: Get the settled basics right everywhere
Set a higher bar for visual craft
Hire more senior designers per team
Move UX earlier in the delivery process
test.explain: The problem isn't the ceiling of ambition; it's basics that keep being got wrong.
